The introduction, read under the orange tree
Thursday, 11 February, in Triana, in the bookshop courtyard. Ecaterina reads Faustino and doña Remedios the first draft of the anthology's introduction.
It begins like this: "It is 30 August. A Madrid newspaper publishes an article about letters nobody has sent."
Why in the present? That happened six months ago.
Because that way the reader is there. The historic present brings what happened closer, as if it were happening now.
Go on. What happens next?
"A few days later, letters begin to arrive. Nobody knows yet that there will be more than four hundred."
I like that. "There will be." As if the reader knew something the characters don't.
And are you going to talk about yourself? About your letter?
I was going to. I was about to write it this morning, when I realised that this book isn't mine.
Then whose is it?
It belongs to the four hundred and twelve. I just open the door. They come in.

For the presentation of Marta's novel, Inés writes a short biography of Faustino in the historic present.

Ecaterina arrived in Seville on Monday, 1 February, on the last train of the afternoon. It was a dry, clean cold, different from the damp cold of Bucharest, and the sky over Triana was an orange colour she didn't remember ever having seen anywhere else. Curro was waiting for her at the station with his mother's car. On the way he told her that Faustino had been preparing the room for three days, that he had gone up and down the stairs so many times that doña Remedios had forbidden him to go up any more, in case he broke a leg before the guest arrived. Ecaterina asked him what Faustino had done in the room. Curro told her she had better see for herself.

The room was on the top floor of the bookshop, at the end of a narrow wooden staircase that creaked on every step. It was small, with white walls, an iron bed, an old wardrobe and a window overlooking the courtyard, where the orange tree, still without blossom, had branches laden with bitter oranges. In front of the window was the new table doña Remedios had promised. On the table, Faustino had placed a blank notebook, three freshly sharpened pencils, an eraser, a lamp with a green shade and, in one corner, propped against the wall, the framed five-hundred-peseta note doña Remedios had received on her wedding day.

Ecaterina asked why the note was there. Doña Remedios, who had come up slowly behind her, holding on to the banister, explained that it had been Faustino's idea. That he said that note was what had started the whole story, and that a woman who was going to write the beginning of a book had to have the beginning of everything in front of her. Ecaterina sat on the bed and looked at the note for a long time. She thought of that afternoon in 1985 on the Cuesta de Moyano, of the debt, of the forty years. She thought that back then she hadn't known that note would end up framed in a room in Triana. Nobody had known. Not even Faustino.

For the first few days she wrote nothing. She got up at seven, when she heard Faustino raising the bookshop's shutter, went down to have breakfast with them in the kitchen, a milky coffee and toast with oil and tomato, and then went up to the room, sat in front of the blank notebook and looked at the orange tree. At midday she came down to eat. In the afternoon she walked around Triana, along calle Betis, across the bridge, through the market. At seven she sat in the bookshop doorway to listen to Faustino read. And at night, before going to sleep, she reread the chosen letters, which she had brought in a folder. Two hundred and twenty-eight letters. She didn't know which one to start with.

Doña Remedios didn't ask her anything for a week. But on Monday the 8th, at breakfast, she told her that she had known many writers in sixty years of bookselling, and that they all had the same problem: they wanted to start at the beginning. Ecaterina asked her where you should start, then. Doña Remedios answered: in the middle, as in life, because nobody starts their life at the beginning: you realise you are alive at four or five, when many things have already happened. Faustino, without looking up from the newspaper, added that he had started his life at eighty-seven. Doña Remedios tapped him on the hand.

That same morning, Ecaterina went up to the room, opened the folder in the middle and took out the first letter she found. It was the one from the woman in Valencia, letter number two hundred, the one in whose margin she had written "the first". Ecaterina smiled. She thought that sometimes things fell into place on their own. And she wrote the first sentence of the introduction, without thinking, in the present: "It is 30 August. A Madrid newspaper publishes an article about letters nobody has sent." She stayed looking at the sentence. She liked it. She wrote the second: "A few days later, letters begin to arrive. Nobody knows yet that there will be more than four hundred." After that she couldn't stop.

She wrote for three days, hardly leaving the room. Doña Remedios brought her coffee up at eleven and lunch at two, on a tray, and left it on the floor outside the door, without knocking, as she had done forty years earlier for a writer from Madrid who had shut himself in that same room to finish a novel he never managed to publish. Faustino, for his part, changed the seven o'clock reading: instead of reading in the doorway, he read in the courtyard, under Ecaterina's window, in a low voice, so as not to disturb her. Ecaterina told him afterwards that she had never written so well as with that voice under the window.

On Thursday the 11th, after dinner, Ecaterina came down to the courtyard with the notebook. Faustino and doña Remedios were sitting under the orange tree, with a blanket over their knees and a butane heater between them. She asked them if she could read them the beginning. Doña Remedios switched off the radio. Ecaterina read the first two sentences. Faustino interrupted to ask her why she had written in the present something that had happened six months ago. Ecaterina explained that this way the reader was there, that the historic present brought what had happened closer, as if it were happening at that moment. Faustino thought about it. He said that was what he did when he told the story of the banknote: he always told it in the present.

Doña Remedios asked her to go on. Ecaterina read the sentence about the four hundred letters. Faustino said he liked that "there will be" very much, because it was as if the reader knew something the characters didn't know yet. Then doña Remedios asked her whether she was going to talk about herself, about her own letter, the one from 1987. Ecaterina answered that she had been going to. That that very morning she had been about to write it when, suddenly, she had realised that this book wasn't hers. Faustino asked her whose it was, then. Ecaterina told him it belonged to the four hundred and twelve. That she just opened the door, and they came in. Doña Remedios said nothing. She took her hand.

The next day a large envelope arrived at the bookshop from Bucharest, with fourteen small envelopes inside. They were letters from the children in the Spanish club, written in class the previous Friday, with Mrs Ionescu's help and under Rosa Elena's strict supervision. Each child had written Ecaterina a letter of three or four sentences, in Spanish, with drawings. Tudor told her he could now say "beben" without thinking. A little girl asked her whether there were cats in Triana. And Rosa Elena's letter said only: "Grandma Ecaterina: it's snowing here. What's happening there? I miss you. Don't forget to come back." Ecaterina put them all up on the wall, above the table.

Meanwhile, in Bucharest, Mr Dan had discovered that a man with a C1 and no exam in sight didn't know what to do with his Thursdays. The first week after passing he was happy. The second he started tidying the garage. The third, Ana found him at the door of the Instituto Cervantes, at five in the afternoon, for no apparent reason. She asked him what he was doing there. Mr Dan confessed he didn't know, that his feet had taken him there by themselves. Ana looked at him for a moment. Then she told him she had a proposal. That the Institute was going to open a conversation group for retired people, on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and needed someone to help them.

Mr Dan asked her if she meant as a student. Ana told him no, she meant as an assistant. That nobody would understand better than him a retired engineer struggling with the subjunctive, or a seventy-year-old lady afraid of making mistakes in front of others. Mr Dan said he wasn't a teacher. Ana reminded him that he had been explaining the subjunctive to Costel for two years in the cab of a truck, with colour-coded tables, and that Costel had passed the C1 before him. Mr Dan was silent. Then he asked what time the first group started. Ana told him the following Tuesday, at five.

Nine students turned up on the first Tuesday. There was a retired doctor, two maths teachers, a former Tarom pilot, a pianist, a lady who had been Ecaterina's neighbour in the eighties and three men who had worked together at a tractor factory. Mr Dan arrived half an hour early, with a folder full of tables. But when the class began, he didn't take any of them out. He told them, in Spanish, slowly, the story of an engineer who had failed the C1 by two points, and of a ninety-seven-year-old man who had told him a lie so that he would sit it again. The students listened in silence. At the end, the pianist applauded.

Ana, who had listened to everything from the doorway, told him afterwards that he had told the story in the present without realising. "An engineer fails the C1. An old man tells him a lie." Mr Dan hadn't noticed. Ana explained that this was exactly what good storytellers did, that the historic present was what made people stay and listen. Mr Dan asked her whether that was in any table. Ana told him no, that this wasn't learned from tables, but in truck cabs and on village porches. Mr Dan wrote the sentence in his notebook, on page two hundred and three.

Costel, meanwhile, had already made his third trip to Valencia. Every time he arrived, the first thing he did, even before going to Irina's, was to stop by Álex's school and take a photo of the walnut tree's patch of earth, next to the green sign, as he had promised Grandpa. The earth was the same: dark, damp, with nothing in it. The biology teacher had explained to him that walnuts were slow to germinate, that they needed the winter cold to wake up, and that nothing would come up until spring. Costel sent the photos to Grandpa anyway. Grandpa looked at them with his glasses on and always said the same thing: that it was asleep, but alive.

On the third trip, Costel did something he hadn't done on the first two. On the way back from Requena, with the empty truck, he took the old road again and stopped at the viewpoint. This time the day was clear, and the sea in the distance was blue, a blue unlike any blue in Romania. He sat on the stone bench and called Ecaterina, who was in Triana, in the upstairs room, writing. He told her the sea was blue. Ecaterina asked him if he was sitting on the bench. Costel told her yes. Ecaterina asked him to stay quiet for a moment, without hanging up. They stayed like that for a minute, each in their own place, listening to the other's silence.

On Monday, 15 February, Andrei arrived in Seville. Begoña had sent him on an assignment: a series for the spring supplement that was going to be called "Writers at their desks", photos of authors in the place where they wrote. Begoña had made a list of twelve Spanish writers. The last name on the list, handwritten, in her small handwriting, was Ecaterina's. Andrei asked Begoña whether that wasn't a bit odd, since Ecaterina was Romanian. Begoña answered that Ecaterina wrote in Spanish at a table in Triana, and that, therefore, she was as much a Spanish writer as any of the other eleven. And that she didn't want to argue about it, because she was in a hurry.

Andrei spent two days in Triana. On the first day he didn't take any photos of Ecaterina. He just watched her. He watched her write in the morning, with the light from the window coming in from the side; he watched her walk along calle Betis in the afternoon; he watched her listen to Faustino at seven in the bookshop doorway. On the second day, at eleven in the morning, he went up with the film camera. Ecaterina was writing and didn't look up. Andrei took a single photo: Ecaterina in profile, bent over the notebook, with her tortoiseshell glasses, the framed note in the corner of the table and, behind her, through the window, the branches of the orange tree full of bitter oranges.

Before going back to Madrid, Andrei sat with Faustino in the bookshop doorway. Faustino asked him about Begoña. Andrei told him about the list of twelve writers and Ecaterina's name handwritten at the end. Faustino laughed. He told him he had known Begoña for thirty years, since she was a young photographer who bought war photography books at his stall, and that he had never seen her do anything by chance. He told him that if she had put Ecaterina last, it was because she wanted the series to end with her. Andrei asked him why. Faustino told him: because Begoña knew, better than anyone, that what matters about a series is how it ends.

The following weekend Pilar came from Cádiz, alone, on the morning train. She was carrying a shoebox wrapped in a plastic bag. She explained to Ecaterina that, finally sorting out her father's wardrobe, she had found behind the coats an old camera, a Zenit from the seventies, with a worn leather case. Inside there was still an undeveloped film. Ecaterina recognised the camera instantly. It was the 1979 camera, the one from the viewpoint, the one of the man passing by. Her hands trembled. Pilar told her she didn't know what to do with it. Ecaterina answered that she did: it had to be sent to Andrei, who knew how to develop film in a darkroom.

Around 20 February, Ecaterina got stuck. She had written six pages: the story of the article, of the boxes, of the letters arriving from all over Spain, of Joaquín and his brother, of the woman from Valencia and her daughter. But she didn't know how to end it. She wrote an ending and crossed it out. She wrote another and crossed that out too. One night doña Remedios heard her pacing the room until two in the morning, making the wooden floor creak. The next morning, at breakfast, she told her to stop looking for the ending, that endings weren't looked for: they were waited for. Ecaterina asked her how long you had to wait. Doña Remedios told her that, in her experience, as long as the orange tree took to blossom.

Andrei received the camera in Madrid three days later, by courier. That same night he shut himself in the agency's darkroom, with Lucas standing guard at the door, so that nobody would open it by mistake. The film was forty years old and most of the photos were fogged, lost forever. But three were saved. One was the La Lámpara bookshop, with its freshly painted green sign. Another was a plate of paella on a terrace table, with two glasses of wine. And the third, slightly out of focus, was the sea, seen from high up, between mountains, with a low stone wall in the foreground. Andrei recognised it immediately. It was the viewpoint. Andrés had taken that photo the very same day.

Ecaterina looked out of the window. The orange tree was the same as on the first day: dark green, with the bitter oranges hanging, without a single flower. Faustino explained to her that Seville's orange trees blossomed in March, sometimes at the end of February if the winter was mild, and that then the whole city smelled of orange blossom for three weeks, so strongly that tourists felt dizzy. Ecaterina said she couldn't wait until March, that she had a return ticket for the 1st. Doña Remedios told her tickets could be changed, and orange trees couldn't. Ecaterina laughed. But that afternoon, just in case, she called the airline and asked how much it cost to change her ticket.

While she waited, she kept reading letters. Every night she reread a dozen, in the iron bed, by the green-shaded lamp. One night she found one she didn't remember choosing. It was very short, written in pencil on a sheet from a school exercise book, in a child's handwriting. It had been written by a twelve-year-old boy from a village in Teruel. He said his grandmother had read him the article aloud, and that he had decided to write a letter to his father, who worked in Germany and came home only twice a year. He didn't say what he had written. He only said, at the end: "My dad's coming back at Christmas. I think he's coming back a bit earlier because I wrote to him."

Ecaterina read that letter three times. Then she got up, put her coat on over her nightdress and went down to the courtyard, although it was one in the morning. She sat on the bench, under the orange tree, in the dark. It was cold. She thought of the boy from Teruel, of his father in Germany, of all the fathers and mothers who worked far away, as Costel had worked on the roads for years while his daughter moved to Valencia. She thought of the boy's sentence: "he's coming back a bit earlier because I wrote to him." She thought that this was exactly what the book wanted to say. And suddenly she knew how the introduction would end. But she didn't go up to write it. She waited.

She waited until Sunday, 28 February, Andalusia Day. That morning, Triana woke up full of green and white flags on the balconies, and from very early there was music in the street. Ecaterina woke at seven, as always, to the sound of the bookshop's shutter. But that morning something was different. It took her a few seconds to realise what. It was the smell. A sweet, intense smell coming in through the gap in the window and filling the whole room. She got up, opened the window and looked down into the courtyard. During the night, without warning, the orange tree had blossomed. The branches were covered in small white flowers.

Ecaterina sat down at the table without getting dressed, in her nightdress and coat, and wrote the ending in one go, in ten minutes, without crossing anything out. She went back to the present, as at the beginning: "Today, in a village in Teruel, a boy is waiting for his father. He doesn't know his letter has made it into a book. His father doesn't know either. But he is coming back a little earlier, because someone wrote to him. This book is for everyone who still has a letter in a drawer. Not so that they publish it: so that they send it." Then she put the pencil down on the notebook, next to the framed note, and sat looking at the orange tree in blossom until doña Remedios came up with the coffee.

Doña Remedios put the tray on the table and didn't ask anything. She saw the open notebook, the pencil on top of it and the window wide open, with the smell of orange blossom pouring in in waves. She went to the window, looked at the orange tree and said, in a low voice, that she had been watching that tree blossom for eighty-four years and had never seen it blossom so early. Ecaterina told her she had finished. Doña Remedios nodded. She told her she already knew, that the orange tree had told her. Then she went down to fetch Faustino. Faustino came up the wooden stairs faster than his doctor allowed, with his red beret in his hand, and stood in the doorway, without coming in, breathing in the orange blossom.

At midday, Ecaterina took a photo of the orange tree in blossom from the window and sent it to Grandpa Gheorghe via Ana. Grandpa replied in the evening, with a voice message Elena had helped him record. He said, in Romanian, that in the village it was still snowing and the walnut tree was white like in Rosa Elena's photo, but that he was glad to know that somewhere in the world it was already spring. And then, in Spanish, with great effort, he said two words he had learned that week with Rosa Elena for the occasion: "Por fin, azahar." Doña Remedios asked them to play the message three times. The third time, she cried.

That afternoon, Andalusia Day, Faustino didn't read a book at random in the bookshop doorway. He read Ecaterina's introduction, all of it, standing, with his beret on, at seven o'clock sharp. More neighbours than ever stopped to listen, because it was a holiday and the street was full. When he reached the sentence about the boy from Teruel, Faustino had to stop for a moment. Then he went on to the end. When he finished, nobody applauded for a few seconds. Then an elderly neighbour, who had lived opposite for fifty years, said aloud that she too had a letter in a drawer. And another neighbour said she did too. And a young man at the back said he had two.

In the evening, as the street emptied, Curro took out his guitar and sat in the courtyard, under the orange tree. First he played some sevillanas, because it was Andalusia Day, and then, without anyone asking, the doina he had learned in August under Grandpa Gheorghe's walnut tree. Ecaterina, at the upstairs window, recognised it by the second note. She came down to the courtyard and sat listening with Faustino and doña Remedios. The orange blossoms fell slowly onto the guitar. Faustino said afterwards that on that night Triana and the Carpathians had shaken hands again, and that this time it had been in his house. Doña Remedios corrected him: in the house of both of them.

That night, Ecaterina called the airline and changed her ticket. Not to stay longer, but to stay just long enough: she would go back to Bucharest on 7 March, a week later, because she wanted to see the orange tree in blossom a few more days, and because doña Remedios had told her that a freshly finished introduction had to be left to rest, like bread, before sending it. Then she called Ana. She told her she had finished. Ana asked her how it ended. Ecaterina told her she wasn't going to tell her over the phone, that she would read it to her in person. Ana asked if she could at least tell her how it began. Ecaterina told her: "It is 30 August."

Before going to sleep, she opened the window one last time. The courtyard was dark, but the smell of orange blossom was so strong you could almost see it. Downstairs, in the kitchen, she heard Faustino and doña Remedios arguing quietly about whether Machado was a better poet than Lorca, as they did every night. In Bucharest, at that hour, Grandpa Gheorghe would already have put out the oil lamp, and in Valencia, under the earth of a school garden, a walnut was still asleep, waiting for spring. Ecaterina thought everything was in its place. She switched off the green-shaded lamp. And, for the first time in many years, she fell asleep without thinking about what she was going to write the next day.

It's the summer of 1998. My mother is twenty and works in an ice-cream shop in Constanța.
One afternoon a shy young man comes in and asks for a lemon ice cream. She doesn't know yet that he will be my father.
He was going to ask her to the cinema that same day, but he didn't dare. He came back the next day, and the day after, and after a week, at last, he spoke to her.
